title: An abelian-variety homomorphism killing prime-to-characteristic torsion is divisible
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $A,B$ be abelian varieties over $k$ [def-sc-abelian-variety], and let $n\geq1$ be an integer invertible in $k$. Let $[n]_A:A\to A$ be multiplication by $n$ [def-sc-mult-n], and put $A[n](k)=\{x\in A(k):[n]_A(x)=0\}$. If a $k$-group-scheme homomorphism $f:A\to B$ [def-sc-group-scheme] satisfies $f(x)=0$ for every $x\in A[n](k)$, there is a unique $k$-group-scheme homomorphism $g:A\to B$ such that $f=g\circ[n]_A$. Equivalently $f=n g$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,B)$, where addition of homomorphisms is pointwise addition in $B$.

source.place: Chapter I, Remark 8.11(f) and Remark 8.12, printed p.39 (quotient universal property for [n]); Lemma 10.16, printed p.49, and its use in Proposition 14.4(b), printed p.62.

proof.text: Write $q=[n]_A$ and $K=A[n]=\ker q$. By [lem-sc-av-commutative], both $A$ and $B$ are commutative group schemes. By [lem-sc-isogeny-facts](a), $q$ is finite, flat and surjective. Since $n\geq1$ is invertible in $k$, [lem-sc-mult-n-etale-kernel] applies and makes $K$ a finite étale group scheme over $k$. This uses the forward implication only, so it also includes the zero-dimensional abelian variety.

The singleton $\{q:A\to A\}$ is an fpqc covering. Indeed, finiteness means in particular that the inverse image of every affine open $V\subset A$ is affine [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. This one affine open $q^{-1}(V)$ maps onto $V$ by surjectivity, and $q$ is flat by step 1. These are exactly the conditions in [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering].

source.place: Tag 022B (definition-fpqc-covering), applied directly; finite morphisms are affine by Morphisms, Tag 01WH.

proof.text: The pointwise hypothesis implies that the restriction $f|_K$ is the zero scheme morphism. To see this without discarding nilpotent information, use the finiteness of $K$ to write $K=\operatorname{Spec}C$, with $C$ a finite $k$-algebra [def-sc-group-scheme]. By [lem-sc-finite-etale-algebra-criterion], $C$ is a finite product of finite separable field extensions of $k$. Every such extension is $k$: the minimal polynomial of any element is irreducible and splits over the algebraically closed field [def-weil-algebraic-closure], hence is linear. Thus $K$ is a finite disjoint union of copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, indexed by $K(k)=A[n](k)$. On each copy the restriction of $f$ is the zero $k$-point by hypothesis; the restrictions therefore assemble to the zero morphism $K\to B$.

source.place: Tag 02GL (lemma-etale-over-field), specialized to a finite scheme over an algebraically closed field; the equivalent finite-algebra classification is lem-sc-finite-etale-algebra-criterion.

proof.text: Check the descent equation explicitly. By the group-scheme operations and the definition of the kernel [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-mult-n], there are inverse scheme morphisms $A\times_k K\longrightarrow A\times_{q,A,q}A$, $(a,t)\longmapsto(a,a+t)$, and $(a,b)\longmapsto(a,b-a)$. The inverse lands in $K$ because $q(b-a)=q(b)-q(a)=0$; the composites are identities by the group laws. The forward map is assembled from the projection, the inclusion $K\to A$ and $m_A$; the reverse uses $m_A$ and inversion, with $q(b-a)=0$ giving its factorization through the defining fibre product for $K$. Thus both maps are scheme morphisms by the fibre-product universal property. Under this identification the two pullbacks of $f$ are $(a,t)\mapsto f(a)$ and $(a,t)\mapsto f(a+t)=f(a)+f(t)$. They are equal as morphisms by step 3. Hence $f\circ\operatorname{pr}_1=f\circ\operatorname{pr}_2$ on the kernel pair of $q$.

source.place: Chapter I, Remarks 8.11(f) and 8.12, printed p.39; scheme-theoretic expansion of the quotient argument used in Lemma 10.16, printed p.49.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] to the covering of step 2, target scheme $B$, and compatible morphism $f$ from step 4. This gives a unique scheme morphism $g:A\to B$ with $g\circ q=f$. It is a $k$-morphism: writing $p_A,p_B$ for the structure maps, $(p_B\circ g)\circ q=p_B\circ f=p_A\circ q$, so uniqueness in the same descent lemma, now with target $\operatorname{Spec}k$, gives $p_B\circ g=p_A$.

source.place: Tag 023Q (lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms), existence and uniqueness of the descended morphism; applied twice.

proof.text: Verify that $g$ is a group homomorphism, using [def-sc-group-scheme]. Let $L=g\circ m_A$ and $R=m_B\circ(g\times g)$ on $A\times_k A$. The maps $h_1=q\times\mathrm{id}$ and $h_2=\mathrm{id}\times q$ are the base changes of $q$ along the first and second projections $A\times_k A\to A$, respectively: the pullback identifications send $(a,b,t)$ with $a=q(t)$ to $(t,b)$, and $(a,b,t)$ with $b=q(t)$ to $(a,t)$. Thus [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change] makes both singleton maps fpqc coverings. Precomposing with $h_1\circ h_2=q\times q$ gives $L(q(a),q(b))=g(q(a+b))=f(a+b)$ and $R(q(a),q(b))=f(a)+f(b)$, equal because $q$ and $f$ are homomorphisms. These are identities of scheme morphisms. Uniqueness in [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] first cancels $h_2$ to give $L\circ h_1=R\circ h_1$, and then cancels $h_1$ to give $L=R$. Also $g\circ e_A=g\circ q\circ e_A=f\circ e_A=e_B$. Finally $(g\circ i_A)\circ q=g\circ q\circ i_A=f\circ i_A=i_B\circ f=(i_B\circ g)\circ q$; uniqueness for $q$ gives $g\circ i_A=i_B\circ g$. Thus $g$ respects all group-scheme operations.

source.place: Tag 022D (lemma-fpqc), part (3), together with Descent Tag 023Q; explicit verification of the homomorphism assertion of Milne, Chapter I, Remark 8.12.

proof.text: The uniqueness in step 5 applies to all scheme morphisms and hence to $k$-group-scheme homomorphisms. Finally, for every $k$-scheme $T$ and $a\in A(T)$, $g_T([n]_A(a))=g_T(na)=n\,g_T(a)$ by the homomorphism law and the definition of multiplication [def-sc-mult-n]. This identifies $g\circ[n]_A$ with the pointwise sum of $n$ copies of $g$ as scheme morphisms. Consequently the factorization is exactly $f=ng$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,B)$.

source.place: Chapter I, Remarks 8.11(f) and 8.12, printed p.39; scheme-theoretic expansion of the quotient argument used in Lemma 10.16, printed p.49.

Step 1: isogeny-facts(a) needs k algebraically closed and n>=1, and gives q=[n] finite, flat and surjective. mult-n-etale-kernel needs char k not dividing n, which holds because n is invertible, and gives A[n] finite étale. Step 2: finite implies affine preimages; with surjectivity and flatness this is exactly the fpqc covering definition. Step 3: by the étale-algebra criterion and algebraic closedness, K is a disjoint union of copies of Spec k, so f restricted to K is the zero scheme morphism. Step 4: the kernel pair is A×K via (a,t)↦(a,a+t), with inverse (a,b)↦(a,b−a). Step 5: one-index fpqc descent gives a unique g, which is a k-morphism by uniqueness into Spec k. Step 6 (changed): h1=q×id and h2=id×q are the base changes of q along the two projections, and the pullback coordinates are right. Cancelling h2 and then h1 gives g∘m_A=m_B∘(g×g), and the identity is preserved. The new inversion clause (g i_A) q = f i_A = i_B f = (i_B g) q is correct; it is redundant but harmless. Step 7: g∘[n]=n·g. I checked the statement against Milne AV I Remark 8.12 (p.39) in the local PDF, and Lemma 10.16 is its general-α form. Edge cases: n=1, f=0 and dimension 0; n=p supersingular shows the invertibility hypothesis is needed.
